replacement: “Besides its being honestly come by, from a ‘sister’ I respect and revere so highly, do you know, I can now look after mamma and Nina, my hunchback angel of a daughter? Doctor Herzenstube came to see us, out of the goodness of his heart, and spent a whole hour examining the two of them. ‘I can’t make anything of it,’ he said. But he prescribed a mineral water, sold at the chemist’s here. He said it would surely do her good, and he ordered baths as well, with some medicine in the water. The mineral water costs thirty kopecks a bottle, and she might need forty of them. So I took the prescription, put it on the shelf under the ikons, and there it lies. And for Nina he ordered hot baths, with something dissolved in them, morning and evening. But how are we to manage a cure like that in our mansion? We have no servants, no help, no bath, not even any water! Nina has rheumatism all over, I don’t think I mentioned that. At night her whole right side aches. She’s in agony, and would you believe it, the angel suffers without a groan, so as not to wake us. We eat whatever we can find, and she will take only the scraps, what you’d hardly throw to a dog. ‘I don’t deserve it, I’m taking it from you, I’m a burden to you,’ that’s what her angel eyes are trying to say. We wait on her, but she hates it. ‘I’m a useless cripple, good for nothing.’ As if she didn’t deserve it, when she is what saves all of us, with her angelic sweetness! Without her, without her gentle word, it would be hell among us! She softens even Varvara. And don’t judge Varvara harshly either. She’s an angel too, and she’s been wronged too. She came to us for the summer with sixteen roubles she had saved from giving lessons, meant for her trip back to Petersburg in September, which is now. But we took her money and lived on it, so now she has nothing to go back with. Not that she could go back anyway, since she has to slave for us here. She’s like an overworked horse with all of us riding on her back. She waits on everyone, mends, washes, sweeps the floor, puts mamma to bed. And mamma is capricious and tearful and out of her mind! But now, with this money, I can hire a servant, you understand, Alexey Fyodorovitch. I can buy medicines for the dear creatures. I can send my student to Petersburg. I can buy beef and feed them properly. Good Lord, it’s a dream!”

And then he ran on without looking back. Alyosha watched him go, grieved beyond words. Oh, he saw that until the very last moment the man had not known he would crush the notes and throw them away. The captain did not turn back, and Alyosha knew he would not. He would not follow or call him back, and he knew why. When the man was out of sight, Alyosha picked up the two notes. They were badly crumpled and had been ground into the sand, but they were not torn. They even rustled like new ones when Alyosha unfolded and smoothed them out. Once he had smoothed them, he folded them, put them in his pocket, and went to Katerina Ivanovna to report on the success of her errand.
